analysis.one_liner: Applies federal workplace laws — discrimination, overtime, safety, leave — to Congress itself.
analysis.headline: Congress voted to end its own exemption from federal workplace laws; the bill passed the Senate 98-1 and the House 390-0 and was signed on January 23, 1995 as Public Law 104-1.
analysis.plain_summary: Before this law, Congress and its offices were exempt from most federal workplace rules — the ones covering discrimination, overtime pay, family and medical leave, workplace safety, and more. The Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 made roughly a dozen of those laws apply to the Senate, the House, and congressional support offices, and created a new Office of Compliance to hear complaints from congressional workers. Congress passed it almost unanimously within its first three weeks and the President signed it.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of thousands of employees who work for the House, Senate, committees, and congressional support agencies — clerks, aides, Capitol Police, cafeteria and maintenance workers — gain the same legal protections against discrimination, unpaid overtime, unsafe conditions, and retaliation that other workers already had, plus a process to enforce them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Congressional employees, from aides to cafeteria workers

how_it_helps.text: Applies Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act to congressional personnel actions, so staffers of every party's office can challenge discrimination based on race, sex, religion, national origin, age, or disability [S3][S4].
Extends the Fair Labor Standards Act to covered congressional employees, guaranteeing minimum wage and overtime rules, and bars paying them compensatory time off in place of overtime pay [S3][S4].

Applies the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Employee Polygraph Protection Act, the WARN Act (60-day notice before mass layoffs), OSHA workplace safety rules, federal labor-management relations, and veterans' reemployment rights to congressional employing offices [S2][S3].

Creates an independent Office of Compliance to educate employing offices, inform workers of their rights, and run counseling, mediation, and hearing procedures, with the right to attorney's fees for workers who prevail [S3][S4].
Makes it unlawful for any congressional employing office to intimidate or retaliate against an employee who files a claim or participates in a proceeding under the Act [S3][S4].

Extends disability-access rules to the Capitol complex and congressional facilities for visitors, guests, and patrons with disabilities, with periodic inspections by the Office's General Counsel [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and the congressional offices that employ staff — personal offices, committees, and support agencies — bear compliance costs: overtime pay, damages to wronged employees, corrective work for safety and disability-access violations, and the loss of the exemption itself. A Treasury account funded by appropriations pays awards and settlements [S3][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and congressional offices

drawbacks.text: The Act bars civil penalties and punitive damages for any claim, so congressional employers face lighter financial consequences than private employers [S3][S4].

Employees must complete the Act's counseling and mediation steps before getting any remedy, and all counseling, mediation, hearing, and Board deliberations are confidential — records generally stay out of public view unless judicial review requires them [S3][S4].

Enforcement is routed through a new Office of Compliance whose regulations require congressional approval, rather than through the Labor Department or the EEOC, and judicial review is limited to what the Act expressly allows [S3][S4].

The labor-management relations provisions leave out the personal offices of Members and committee staff until Board regulations are issued, and explicitly allow considering party affiliation and political compatibility in hiring for Member, committee, and leadership staff [S3][S4].

The House and Senate ethics committees keep full power to discipline Members under their own nondiscrimination rules, so Members themselves are still judged by their colleagues rather than an outside body [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and went to a group of workers — congressional employees — who previously had almost no recourse against discrimination, unpaid overtime, or unsafe conditions in their own workplace. The design compromises are meaningful: no punitive damages, a mandatory counseling-and-mediation gate before any remedy, confidential proceedings, and enforcement through a new in-house office whose regulations Congress itself approves. The result is protection for congressional workers, but on gentler terms than the same workers would get in a private-sector job.

outcome.mechanism: It sailed through both chambers by near-unanimous votes in Congress's first three weeks — 98-1 in the Senate on January 11 and 390-0 in the House on January 17 — and the President signed it on January 23, 1995 as Public Law 104-1.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress, and it was placed on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 1 [S1][S5].
It had 39 cosponsors in the Senate — 27 Republicans and 12 Democrats — before consideration began [S5].
The Senate debated it for several days and passed it on January 11, 1995 by a vote of 98-1, with all 53 Republicans in favor and 45 of 47 Democrats in favor [S6][S7].
On January 12 the Senate incorporated the measure into the companion H.R. 1 and passed H.R. 1 by unanimous consent, sending it to the House [S6].
The House passed the bill under a procedure reserved for noncontroversial measures on January 17, 1995, 390-0, with every voting member in favor [S6][S8].
The President signed it on January 23, 1995, making it Public Law 104-1 — the first law enacted by the 104th Congress [S4][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Congressional employees came out ahead: they gained enforceable workplace rights they had never had. Members of Congress and congressional offices gave up their exemption and took on compliance costs, but both parties shared that cost equally, and no organized interest lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Congressional employees, who gained workplace rights

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 on the first day of the 104th Congress and managed its Senate consideration.

for.name: 27 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 53 Republican senators then voted yes on final passage.

for.name: 12 of 47 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; 45 of 47 Democratic senators voted yes on final passage.

for.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill in the House, bringing it to a floor vote three days after Senate passage.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on January 23, 1995 as Public Law 104-1.

sides.party_line_note: There was no opposition to speak of: the Senate passed it 98-1 (all 53 Republicans and 45 of 47 Democrats in favor) and the House passed it 390-0, with Republicans and Democrats voting yes in equal proportion.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and congressional employing offices (personal offices, committees, and support agencies)
industries.note: The bill stripped Congress's self-exemption from workplace laws, requiring Members' offices, committees, and agencies to pay overtime, accommodate disabilities, fix safety hazards, and answer for discrimination claims. Their interest in keeping the exemption ran directly against the rights of the people who work for them.

industries.industry: Federal workplace-law enforcement agencies (Labor Department, EEOC, Federal Labor Relations Authority)
industries.note: Their substantive standards were extended to Congress, but enforcement was routed to the new Office of Compliance instead, with the Board exercising powers these agencies normally hold over their own branch. They gained the norm but not the jurisdiction.
